scenes.narration: You know the patterns. The interview hands you a problem. Where does the method go?
This is the Dojo, from THE NBX STUDIO, and this is the method the whole series runs on: six steps, in order, that take you from a question you've never seen to code you can defend.

scenes.headline: Six steps, [in order]
scenes.caption: the whole method
scenes.narration: Here are all six, and the order genuinely matters. ^Read and draw. ^Spot the signals. ^Match the pattern. ^Plan in plain English. ^Code it clean. ^Test and analyse. Most candidates start at step five, because writing code feels like progress and staring at a problem feels like failing at it. But interviewers grade steps one to four at least as hard as the code, and often harder.

cells.sub: the words that give it away

cells.label: Test and analyse
cells.sub: trace it, then state the cost

scenes.premise: The six steps, run in order on any question you are handed. Read the symptoms first, choose the treatment second.

scenes.headline: One · [read and draw]
scenes.caption: before anything else
scenes.narration: ^Read the problem three times, and I mean literally three. Not twice: people miss a constraint on the first pass and invent one on the second. ^Then draw the input and the output, physically, on paper. ^Write the edge cases down before you forget them: empty, single element, duplicates, negatives. ^Finish by saying what's being asked, in your own words. ^If you can't say that sentence, no amount of code will rescue you.

cells.label: read it three times
cells.sub: once is how you miss a constraint

cells.label: say it in your own words
cannot say it?
cells.sub: then you cannot pick a pattern

scenes.premise: The six steps, run in order on any question you are handed. Read the symptoms first, choose the treatment second.

scenes.headline: Two · [spot the signals]
scenes.caption: the words are the cheat code
scenes.narration: Step two is what this whole series is built around. Problems announce their own pattern, and the announcement is usually a single word. ^Sorted. ^Contiguous. ^All combinations. ^Shortest. ^Frequency. ^Nested. Read the question again with a pen and circle the nouns and adjectives that constrain the input, because those words carry the pattern. Verbs tell you what to return; constraints tell you how to get there.
scenes.premise: Words lifted straight out of the question, and the pattern each one points at. Red means the signal rules this pattern OUT.

scenes.headline: Three · [match the pattern]
scenes.caption: one or two candidates, not ten
scenes.narration: ^From the signals, name one or two candidate patterns. Not ten, and not none. ^Then ask honestly whether that pattern's core idea applies here. Two pointers works only because sorted lets you eliminate a whole side; with nothing sorted, the reasoning collapses. ^Say your candidate out loud: this looks like a sliding window, because the question says contiguous. ^Wrong out loud is recoverable and invites a hint. ^Four silent minutes is not. Interviewers can't give you credit for thinking they never heard.

cells.label: say it out loud
cells.sub: name the pattern and the signal

scenes.premise: The six steps, run in order on any question you are handed. Read the symptoms first, choose the treatment second.

scenes.headline: Four · [plan in plain English]
scenes.caption: the step people skip
scenes.narration: This is the step candidates skip, and it's the one that changes the outcome. ^Explain the approach in plain English before writing anything. ^Then walk your own example through it by hand, out loud. ^You'll catch half your bugs here, for free, because tracing an idea is faster than debugging code. ^An interviewer who heard a clear plan forgives a syntax error.

cells.label: catch bugs while they are free

scenes.premise: The six steps, run in order on any question you are handed. Read the symptoms first, choose the treatment second.

scenes.narration: ^Quick one. You've read the problem, the array is sorted, and it asks for a pair. What next? ^Start writing the two-pointer code. ^Say the pattern out loud and walk an example. ^Or check whether a hash map is faster. Have a think, and pause if you'd like. ^Ready? Say it and walk an example, because the plan is what's being graded and it's cheap to change.

scenes.headline: Five · [code it clean]
scenes.caption: now, and not before
scenes.narration: ^Now you write it, and the goal is readable rather than clever. ^Use names a stranger could follow: left and right, not i and j, when left and right is what they actually mean. ^Start with the simple version that works. ^Don't optimise while you type, because premature optimisation reads as uncertainty, ^and speeding up correct code is far easier than correcting fast code.

cells.label: readable beats clever
cells.sub: a stranger has to follow it

cells.label: name things properly
cells.sub: left and right, not i and j

scenes.premise: The six steps, run in order on any question you are handed. Read the symptoms first, choose the treatment second.

scenes.headline: Six · [test and analyse]
scenes.caption: finish properly
scenes.narration: ^Trace your own code with the example, out loud. Find your own bug rather than letting the interviewer find it, because one of those looks considerably better. ^Then run the edge cases from step one. ^State your time and space complexity without being asked. ^Ten seconds, ^and the difference between finished and abandoned. Say the two values and stop, because nobody wants a lecture at the end of an interview.
scenes.premise: The six steps, run in order on any question you are handed. Read the symptoms first, choose the treatment second.

scenes.headline: The whole [signal table]
scenes.caption: ten patterns, one page
scenes.narration: Here's the table this whole series builds, and it's worth writing out by hand once. ^Sorted plus a pair means two pointers. ^Contiguous, or subarray, means sliding window. ^Sorted plus find means binary search. ^Frequency, or have I seen this, means a hash map. ^Nested, or brackets, means a stack. ^Shortest, or fewest steps, means breadth-first search. ^All combinations means backtracking. ^Number of ways, or minimum cost, is dynamic programming. ^Intervals or scheduling means sort, then greedy. ^And cycle, or the middle, means fast and slow pointers. Ten rows. Copy them onto one card and read the card before every practice session.

scenes.narration: Three things to take with you. %Read before you reach, because a pattern chosen from half a problem is a wrong pattern. %The signals are in the question, and circling them is a real technique. And %say the plan out loud, because the plan is what's actually being graded.
